KEY MESSAGE 1...
High pressure continues to move east of New England this
afternoon, as a warm front approaches from the lower Great Lakes
Region and Ohio Valley. A short-wave trough lifts
north/northeast towards the Piedmont/Mid Atlantic Region
tonight. The isentropic lift increases ahead of the warm front 
for showers to break out and few t-storms ahead of the boundary 
tonight initially north and west of the Capital Region, and then
expanding south and east across the region as a weak low tracks
towards Long Island. Showalter index values lower to 0 to -2C 
on the NAM/EC and the latest mean MUCAPEs from the HREFS are 
generally <300 J/kg. Elevated instability is present. PWATs rise
+1 to +3 STDEVS above normal into the 1.5-2.0" range with 
highest values values south and east of the Capital Region 
towards I-84. Some dynamical support from the right entrance 
region of an upper level jet streak over southeast 
Quebec/northern NY will help enhance the rainfall overnight 
coupled with efficient warm rainfall processes with high 
freezing levels or warm cloud depths. Some of the guidance 
continues to show some low/mid-level FGEN, but varies in the 
placement. The latest 3-km NAM looks like an outlier with a QPF 
bullseye of a few inches further north to the northern reaches 
of the Capital Region/Saratoga Region/srn VT. An uptick of QPF 
is supported by the CAMs and WPC and we have a half an inch to 
an inch from the Capital Region north and west with slightly 
lower amounts over the southern Dacks to account for any bands 
of heavy showers/t-storms. 

The heavier rainfall amounts still look to be south and east of
I-90 towards the mid Hudson Valley/NW CT and the southeast
Catskills towards the I-84 corridor with 1-1.5" with locally
higher amounts of 2" or so. The good news is that gridded FFG 
values in these areas are 1.8-2.5"/hr or 2.5-3.5"/3 hrs. The 
6-hr FFG values are mainly 3-5"/6 hr in these areas. Latest 
HREFs indicates the heaviest rainfall for the southern most 
areas would be in the 12Z-18Z (8 am to 2 pm)/Sun time frame 
with probs >1" in 6 hrs 30-40% for portions of Dutchess, 
Berkshires and Litchfield Counties. 2" and 3" probs/6 hrs are 
lower. These same areas 12Z-15Z (8 to 11 am) Sun indicate 
rainfall probs >1" 70-90%; 50-70% up to the Capital 
Region/northern Taconics/southern VT and >3" rainfall in 3-hrs 
only 10-20% for portions of the mid Hudson Valley, southern 
Taconics and Litchfield Hills, NW CT. Ponding of water on 
roadways, poor drainage flooding of low-lying and urban areas 
looks like the greatest threats still. Rainfall rates may 
briefly peak at 0.5-1"/hr. The dry antecedent conditions will 
also help keep the flash flood threat low. Isolated flash 
flooding can not be ruled out in these areas (closer to I-84 and
the mid Hudson valley/southern Taconics/NW CT south and east), 
where the Marginal Risk is in effect tonight into early tomorrow
morning. A ERO Day 2 Slight Risk glances southern Litchfield Co
in Day 2. The rainfall should diminish in the late morning. 
Lows fall back into the 50s to lower 60s 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Clouds will begin the day from most of the region. A lull in 
the rainfall is expected from the late morning into the early to
mid pm. A prefrontal sfc trough and a cold front will be 
approaching from the west. Dewpoints will be in the 60s to 
around 70F in a few spots. The cold front is associated with a 
strong mid and upper level trough. Isolated- scattered showers 
and isolated- widely scattered thunderstorms will likely develop
in the mid- late pm into the evening from northwest to 
southeast across the forecast area. CAMS continue to struggle in
convective initiation and coverage. The best chance for some 
stronger storms to develop may be from the Capital Region and 
southern VT north and west associated with heights falls aloft 
and mean SBCAPEs on the HREFs are in the 750-1250 J/kg range 
with 0-6 km shear around 40-45 KT. The mid level lapse rates 
look marginal at 6-6.5C/km in these areas. The timing does not 
look great for a widespread severe threat, but an isolated 
threat with a few storms with damaging winds/marginal hail if 
enough heating and the better shear/CAPE overlap with the 
frontal forcing/upper level support. The better chance of 
showers and thunderstorms across the majority of the region 
looks like the late pm and night time period prior to midnight 
with the mid and upper level jet moving across southeast Canada.
SPC continues the Marginal Risk for most of eastern NY and 
western New England (mainly north and west of the mid-Hudson 
valley, southern Taconics and NW CT). In the wake of the front. 
Strong cold advection occurs and it will become breezy and less 
humid. Lows in the 50s to around 60F with some mid/upper 40s in 
the southern Dacks. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...

A cooler and drier air mass returns to open the week. Dewpoints
fall in the 40s to lower 50s on Monday. It will become breezy
with west/northwest winds 10-15 mp
